OPEC+ leaves its December quotas alone: oil stays hostage to the Gulf war

Meeting on Sunday, November 1, the seven countries that steer OPEC+ output kept their December quotas unchanged, at about 31.01 million barrels a day. It is the third month in a row on hold, while most Gulf producers can no longer reach their targets anyway [1][2][4].

The seven countries involved (Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman) decided to hold their required output in December at about 31.01 million barrels a day, the September level [2][4].
For the biggest of them, that means about 10.48 million barrels a day for Saudi Arabia, 9.95 for Russia and 4.43 for Iraq [2][3].
It is the third consecutive month on hold: the group had raised its quotas every month from April to September, then froze them for October and for November [2][5].

The move is mostly symbolic: Gulf producers are pumping well below their targets because their exports are still hampered by the war with Iran. According to Reuters sources, they have been running at 60 to 80% of normal for several months [1].
OPEC's figures confirm it: in August the seven countries produced 25 million barrels a day, 630,000 more than in July but still about 5 million less than in February, before the war [5].
The price of a barrel remains very high: Brent was still above $114 on October 29, according to AFP, with moves driven mostly by diplomatic signals between Washington and Tehran [6].

The key point: normally an OPEC+ decision moves the oil price; this time it matters almost less than the Strait of Hormuz. When a quota is higher than what countries can actually produce, raising or lowering it changes nothing about the barrels sold. That is exactly Sunday's situation: the constraint comes from export routes, not from the group's decision [1][5].

The real appointment is the big meeting of the alliance's 21 members, planned for November 29, where 2027 quotas are expected to be set. Reuters stresses that the war makes this work hard: each country's future output has to be estimated once the conflict is over, while facilities and routes are still disrupted [1].

For producing countries the bill is double. They benefit from an expensive barrel but export less than planned; for importing countries, such as those in Europe and Asia, high energy prices weigh on production, transport and households. A return of Gulf exports, for example after a deal on Hormuz, would instead bring prices down [1][6].

As long as Gulf production is hampered, the price of petrol and diesel is tied to news about Hormuz far more than to OPEC+ meetings. November 29 will be the next moment when 2027 quotas, and so next year's fuel price, can move.

Vietnam passes $1 trillion in trade, but Washington must rule on tariffs on November 29

Over ten months, Vietnam's foreign trade reaches about $1,010.6 billion, 32.3% more than a year earlier. At the same time, the United States must deliver on November 29 its decision on an investigation that could lead to new tariffs on Hanoi [1][2][3].

According to Vietnam's Ministry of Industry and Trade, trade in goods (exports plus imports) reached about $1,010.6 billion from January to October 2026, 32.3% more than over the same period of 2025 [1].
This success has a downside, which the Vietnamese press points out: the share of value actually created in the country stays low, because factories assemble a lot of imported parts [1].

On May 29, 2026 the United States opened a so-called “Section 301” investigation into how Vietnam protects intellectual property (trademarks, patents, counterfeits). In April it had already been named a “priority foreign country” in the US Trade Representative's annual report, a first since 2013 [3][5].
The final decision is due by November 29, 2026 at the latest; it may come with tariffs or other trade measures [2][3].
Hanoi disputes the accusations and points to a new intellectual property law that took effect in December 2025 [3].

Companies oppose new duties: Tesla cites US manufacturers' supply-chain needs, and Samsung notes that Vietnam is a key base for smartphones and network equipment sold in the United States. According to Reuters, business circles are split over whether to propose them this month [2].

The key point: Vietnam has become one of the world's factories, and that is what exposes it. When companies looked to produce somewhere other than China, some chose Vietnam; its trade now exceeds $1 trillion in ten months, up 32.3% [1].

For Washington, a Section 301 investigation is a fast tool: it lets the government impose tariffs without going through Congress, provided it shows practices judged unfair. Here the official argument is about intellectual property: trademarks, patents and counterfeits [3][5].

The dilemma shows in the companies' positions: taxing Vietnamese products also makes products made by American groups or their suppliers more expensive. That explains why business circles are divided [2].
Clothes, shoes, furniture and electronics sold in Europe are made in Vietnam. New US tariffs could divert some of these goods to Europe, or push their prices up, depending on Hanoi's reaction.

Chevron earns $10.4 billion in three months thanks to refining, and aims to double its oil in Venezuela

US oil giant Chevron announced on October 30 an adjusted profit of $10.4 billion for the third quarter, or $5.28 a share, more than expected. It is its refineries, which benefit from expensive diesel, more than the price of crude that drive the result [1][2][4].
Chevron published an adjusted profit of $10.4 billion for the third quarter, or $5.28 a share; counting exceptional items, profit reaches $9.9 billion, or $5.06 a share [1][2].
Analysts expected $4.83 a share and the group had earned $1.85 a year earlier [4].

It is the downstream activities, that is refining, that drive the result: margins rose and US refineries ran at a record level to take advantage of high diesel prices. Conversely, extraction results fell, because crude selling prices were lower [2][4].

The group reports records: output of about 3.98 million barrels of oil equivalent a day, natural gas above 9 billion cubic feet a day, and more than 2 million barrels a day in the United States for the fifth quarter in a row [2].
Free cash flow reaches $14.2 billion for the quarter [2][3]. Adjusted profit is, however, $1.6 billion lower than in the previous quarter [2].

Chevron also presents a plan to double its output in Venezuela, to 600,000 barrels a day by 2031, at a production cost under $20 a barrel [2][3]. According to the Financial Times, Exxon and Chevron together made $25.3 billion of net profit over the quarter [7].

The key point: when oil is expensive because of a war, it is not always the wells that earn the most. Here, crude prices weighed on extraction, but diesel stayed expensive: refiners, who turn crude into fuel, pocket the gap between the two. Exxon said refining margins added about $4.5 billion to its profit, while the crude price reduced it by $1.3 billion [4].

The Venezuelan plan is the most political fact of this result: Chevron says it wants to double its production in Venezuela, to 600,000 barrels a day by 2031, at under $20 a barrel. It is a long-term project, which will depend on the country's political and legal framework [2][3].

For investors the question is whether these profits last. They rest partly on expensive fuel; if prices fell, refining margins would narrow. That is the classic oil-company mechanism: their results rise when energy is expensive, and fall back when it normalizes [4][6].

When you fill up, the expensive diesel you pay is exactly what inflates these profits. If your savings are in a global fund, the big oil companies are part of it: their results therefore matter for your portfolio too.

How it works: why an oil company earns money even when crude falls

A company like Chevron does two jobs. Upstream, it extracts oil and gas, and earns according to the price of a barrel. Downstream, it refines: it buys crude, turns it into diesel, petrol or jet fuel, and earns the gap (the refining margin) between the price of fuels and that of crude. When diesel is more expensive than the crude it is made from, the margin climbs and refineries earn a lot, even if the barrel price weighs on extraction. That is what this quarter shows: refining pushed Chevron's results up, extraction pulled them down [2][4].

news.2026-11-02-philippines-pas-de-sanct: Philippines: Manila rules out punishing Beijing through trade, despite South China Sea tensions

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. refuses to resort to trade sanctions or export restrictions against China. The country depends on Beijing for 28.6% of its imports, or $38.44 billion in 2025 [1][2].

Asked about a possible restriction on nickel exports from Surigao del Sur province to China, presidential spokesperson Claire Castro ruled out any trade retaliation. The palace separates economic ties from the defense of territory [1][2].
China is the Philippines' biggest source of imports: $38.44 billion of goods in 2025, or 28.6% of the total [1].
The country exported $994.1 million of nickel ore and concentrates to China in 2025, against $808.6 million a year earlier, according to UN data compiled by the World Bank [1].
Authorities fear that worsening relations would disrupt industry and exports, because many sectors use Chinese raw materials and components [1].

The key point: a country can be in military tension with its first supplier and still refuse to cut trade, because the bill would fall on itself. The Philippines depends on China for more than a quarter of its imports, which limits its means of pressure [1].

The position is all the more notable as Beijing reminded Manila on October 22 to respect the one-China principle, while the Philippines is getting closer to Taiwan to deal with so-called “gray zone” activities at sea [3].
Nickel is a battery metal: a trade break between Manila and Beijing could affect the prices of products you buy, from electronics to electric vehicles.

news.2026-11-02-espagne-legislatives-29-: Spain: a month before the November 29 election, housing drives the campaign

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called an early election for November 29, after Congress rejected two housing decrees. The polls cited put the People's Party and Vox together above 200 seats out of 350 [1][2][3].
On October 2, the Congress of Deputies rejected two government decrees meant to limit evictions and real-estate speculation; right-wing parties voted against together [3][4].
On October 5, Pedro Sánchez announced in a televised address an early general election for November 29 [1][2].
The vote was normally due by August 2027 at the latest [3].
According to polls cited by the Bernama agency, the People's Party (right) and Vox (far right) together would win more than 200 of the 350 seats in Congress [3].

The key point: housing has become Spain's number one political issue. The rejected decrees aimed to protect tenants, and Sánchez is betting that anger over rents can serve as a campaign argument [1][2][4].

For the economy, the stake is the stability of a country that, according to recent forecasts, is growing faster than Germany, France and Italy: a right-wing coalition could change housing policy and public spending policy [5].
If you rent or buy in Spain, the November 29 result matters: the new government will decide housing policy, that is the rules on rents and evictions.
